The person who governs all of New Hampshire's public universities could also be the leader of its largest, after a recommendation by the organization overseeing them. The University System of New Hampshire's Board of Trustees held a vote June 25-26 in favor of the recommendation. If state lawmakers approve, it would merge the roles of USNH chancellor and University of New Hampshire president into a single position. The president would also serve as chancellor overseeing Keene State College and Plymouth State University, the two other schools under the USNH umbrella, with both schools' presidents reporting to that office. The change would modify the current law under Chapter 187-A, which sets parameters for state colleges. All three institutions would remain separate. >> Download the free WMUR app to get updates on the go << Current chancellor Catherine Provencher said she and the presidents of all three schools were tasked in March with coming up with an idea to improve future leadership. UNH enrolls 70% of the system's students, and accounts for 80% of its costs. Provencher said out of all three schools, the university's scale made it the logical home for shared services now housed in the Chancellor's office. Human resources, procurement, and accounting could also have additional staff if the organization sees it as beneficial. The recommendation comes as New Hampshire's public universities face financial pressure and sinking enrollment. The state ranks last in the nation for public higher education funding, according to the New Hampshire Fiscal Policy Institute. The number of students attending class has also gone down, as fewer traditional college-age students choose four-year institutions. Provencher said the consolidation would improve the speed of decision-making and overall efficiency, without sacrificing independence. "It will align business processes and practices for consistency across our entire enterprise," Provencher said. "Then we can build strength across all three institutions." Provencher said USNH consulted with other university systems around the country that already operate under the proposed model, including the University of Houston system and Washington state's system. She emphasized that the change would not amount to folding the smaller schools into UNH. "Those institutions are integral to the economic health of those regions of our state and our state as a whole," she said. George Hansel, a USNH trustee, voted against the recommendation. He said the proposal raises unanswered questions about how one person can balance the needs of a large university with two smaller campuses. "There is an urgent need for change. No one is denying that," Hansel said. "(But) I think there are multiple solutions, or multiple things, that our institutions need to do to innovate and remain relevant." Hansel said his main concern was preserving the autonomy of Keene State and Plymouth State. "I want to make sure as a trustee, that each of our individual institutions has the room to run, the room to innovate, and come up with a path that really just serves the needs of their local communities," he said. He added that he welcomes the legislature's involvement, as it would open up broader conversations about the decision. "We do have to be careful as we move forward and make sure we're really thinking about this holistically and in a way that allows us to utilize the fact that we're a small state with a small system," Hansel said. The New Hampshire Legislature needs to approve the changes before the merger can take effect. If cleared, the positions would combine on July 1, 2027. title: UNH lands $8M grant to study ticks and tickborne diseases - New Hampshire Public Radio
content: This story was originally produced by the New Hampshire Bulletin, an independent local newsroom that allows NHPR and other outlets to republish its reporting. New Hampshire’s ticks are having a moment, prompting the state’s scientists to come together in hopes of better understanding, and combating, the problem. An $8 million grant from the National Science Foundation will support an investigation into how factors like climate, habitat, wildlife, and more affect the parasites and the diseases they spread, according to a release shared by the University of New Hampshire on Wednesday. “Ticks are an issue that touches nearly every community in New Hampshire,” said David Needle, a University of New Hampshire professor and veterinary pathologist leading the four-year project, in the release. Scientists from the University of New Hampshire, Keene State University, and Plymouth State University, and students, state agencies, and private industry will collaborate on the initiative. The announcement comes as ticks, and the various illnesses they carry, pose an increasing risk to the health of humans and wildlife alike. Emergency room visits for tick bites surged this summer, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. And while tick-borne illnesses that have been increasingly common for decades, like Lyme disease, remain both prevalent and dangerous, diseases that have emerged more recently are on the rise, too. Warmer winters, driven by climate change, have helped tick populations gain ground, aided by development and shifts in wildlife populations, according to the release. Scientists participating in the study will come from various fields to participate in the project, according to the release. Areas of inquiry are set to include studying ticks and the pathogens they carry through the lenses of genomics, the study and comparison of entire genome sequences; ecology; data science; and utilizing artificial intelligence. Studying ticks can shed light on systems larger than themselves, Needle said in the release, giving the study the potential to build understanding not only of tick-borne illnesses but of other complex, interconnected systems, too. title: UNH awarded $8M grant to study ticks - WMUR

The University of New Hampshire is getting an $8 million grant to study ticks, the diseases they spread and the environments they thrive in. The grant from the National Science Foundation comes at a time when concern is high about tick-borne illnesses and the spread of additional tick species into the region. Recent research shows that ticks are also showing up in more cities along the East Coast, not just in wooded areas. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, New Hampshire has one of the highest rates of Lyme disease in the country. "They come in the first season, and then you're like, 'Oh they're gone.' And then October, November, you go outside, and there's ticks all over the place again," said David Needle, a clinical professor and senior veterinary pathologist who will lead the four-year initiative. "But, we're using that as like an annually renewable resource, like a repeated experiment that's there for us." The funding will focus on three tick species found in New Hampshire: the blacklegged or deer tick, the American dog tick and the winter tick, which has major impacts on moose and wildlife health. >> Download the free WMUR app to get updates on the go << Researchers will investigate how ticks survive, spread and transmit disease by setting up 22 stations across the state. "From those stations, we will drag for ticks during peak season," said Needle. "The stations will monitor all year round, and so we can get deeper into the question of, like, what does snow coverage do?" Needle said that portion of the research will start at the beginning of the next peak season. Thousands of people get Lyme disease every year, and ticks are known to be a menace in New Hampshire as the disease they carry requires extra precautions. "It's been a difficult time because I live in Dunbarton, so I live in like, the woody area," said Kennith Dibattista of Dunbarton. Pets, such as dogs, also require prevention from tickborne illnesses. "You know, it was really, really bad last year, so I decided to do the heartworm plus the tick preventative monthly pill, as well as the collars that prevent ticks as well," said Chantel McMillan of Manchester. The multimillion-dollar grant also has an educational component, as undergraduate students from across the Granite State will assist with the research. content:

As tick numbers show no sign of decreasing and the types of diseases they can spread to people keep increasing, a new initiative has been launched to figure out other ways we can respond beyond tucking our pants into our socks when walking through tall grass. UNH on Thursday announced an $8 million grant from the National Science Foundation for the university to launch a statewide research and education initiative focused on ticks, the diseases they carry, and their impact on people, wildlife and the environment. The effort, given the mouthful of an acronym, EMBEDDEd-NH (Endeavor for Multi-Omics-Based Exploration, Data-Driven Modeling, and Education in New Hampshire), comes as New Hampshire consistently ranks among the states with the highest incidence of Lyme disease, the most common tick-borne disease in the Northeast. “By combining cutting-edge science with statewide collaboration and education, we have an opportunity to build knowledge that benefits both our state and the broader scientific community,” said Dr. David Needle, clinical professor of molecular, cellular and biomedical Sciences and senior veterinary pathologist of the New Hampshire Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory at UNH. This comes as the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says emergency room visits for tick bites in April were the highest for that time of year since 2017. Health officials are increasingly concerned about the emergence of new pathogens and the spread of additional tick species into the region. New England has seen that with the continuing increase in Powassan virus spread by ticks, which has contributed to the death of at least one person in the state this year, as well as the arrival in southern New England of the Lone Star tick, which is moving north as climate change makes winters milder and summers hotter. Award-winning coverage on breaking news and today’s top stories in and around the Capital Region. From Arts and Life to Sports and Opinion you’ll have unlimited access to the Concord Monitor's content. Recent research shows that ticks are also showing up more in cities along the East Coast, not just in wooded areas. Warmer winters, changing land use, shifting wildlife populations and expanding human development have all contributed. Work is proceeding on a human vaccine for Lyme disease, although one is still years away and would not do anything about other diseases spread by ticks. Health officials have long said that the best response to ticks is to avoid getting bitten. When outdoors in tick territory, wearing long-sleeve shirts and long pants tucked into your socks so ticks can’t crawl up your leg is an important first step. Ticks grab onto people as they walk past; they do not drop down from trees because they have terrible vision and don’t know you’re around unless they feel vibrations from your walking. However, they can crawl very quickly once they get on you, which is how they end up in our hair. Other prevention measures include putting tick insecticide such as permethrin on clothing — not directly on skin — and checking yourself very carefully for ticks after you come indoors, especially in spring and fall when they are most active. The UNH initiative will focus on blacklegged ticks, also called deer ticks, which are the major spreader of disease to humans; the American dog tick; and the winter tick, which doesn’t bother people but has exploded in numbers and is threatening the region’s moose population. Needle is leading the four-year study that includes experts in genomics, ecology, and artificial intelligence, as well as an opportunity for undergraduate involvement. Researchers plan to investigate how ticks survive, spread, and transmit disease by using genomic sequencing, microbiome analysis, environmental monitoring, ecological modeling, and machine learning. They will examine how climate, habitat, wildlife hosts, and microbial communities influence tick biology and pathogen transmission across New Hampshire’s ecosystems. “Ticks are more than just disease vectors,” Needle said. “They have wide roles as parasites, prey, and hosts of diverse microbes.” The initiative will include researchers, students, and community partners from the University of New Hampshire, Keene State College, Plymouth State University, state agencies, and industry collaborators. The initiative also places a major emphasis on education and workforce development. UNH also offers tick testing to the public through UNH Extension. The service can detect the presence of a pathogen in a tick in as little as three days. For more information, go to unh.how/tick. EMBEDDed-NH is supported by funding from the National Science Foundation’s EPSCoR E-RISE program, which supports statewide research infrastructure, workforce development, and collaborative scientific innovation in emerging research areas. title: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez jumps to front of NH 2028 Dem primary field - Seacoastonline.com
content: In the latest snapshot of the 2028 presidential race, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-NY, now leads the potential 2028 Democratic primary field in New Hampshire, surpassing former Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg for the first time since the University of New Hampshire Survey Center started polling the race in October 2025. The result follows a late June Saint Anselm poll that found Ocasio-Cortez had surged, but hadn't taken over Buttigieg's lead. The new UNH poll, released July 22, found that 22% of likely 2028 Democratic primary voters said they would vote for Ocasio-Cortez, up from 15% in February. She is followed closely by Buttigieg: 21% said they would vote for him, up from 20% in February. Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Arizona, has also moved up from tied for seventh in October to third in July with 9% support, followed by California Gov. Gavin Newsom at 8% and Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-VT, with 6%. Ocasio-Cortez draws her support from socialists and progressives, and people who support her most often say cite her policies, politics or ideology, or age. Buttigieg is propelled by liberals and moderates, and people who support him most often cite his competence or qualifications, authenticity or honesty, or character. Ocasio-Cortez is also the most popular potential candidate, with 64% having a favorable opinion of her versus 9% who have an unfavorable opinion, giving her a net favorability of +55 among Democratic primary voters. Buttigieg follows closely, with a +54 favorability rating. The poll surveyed 1,458 New Hampshire residents between July 15 and July 20. The margin of error is +/-2.6%. No candidates, including Ocasio-Cortez, have declared their candidacy for president yet with the election still over two years away. But there’s been speculation over whether the New York congresswoman will run, In May, she dodged a question about whether she will run for Senate or president in 2028. "They assume that my ambition is a title or a seat," Ocasio-Cortez said. "And my ambition is way bigger than that. My ambition is to change this country." In June, Vice President JD Vance said in an interview on "The Michael Knowles Show" that he thought Ocasio-Cortez would be the leading Democratic candidate. In response, she said that she hopes he’s the Republican nominee. Vance continues to lead the 2028 Republican primary, but Secretary of State Marco Rubio has gained significant ground since February. The poll found 36% of likely 2028 Republican primary voters say they would vote for Vance if the election was held today, while 26% would vote for Rubio. In February, Vance led with 53%, followed by former UN Ambassador Nikki Haley at 9% and Rubio at 7%. People who support Vance most often cite his qualifications or competence, values, and past experience. Similarly, people who support Rubio most often cite his experience, qualifications or competence, and his policies. Vance is also the most popular potential candidate in New Hampshire among their party's voters, according to the poll, with a net approval rating of +62 among Republicans. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and Rubio are the next most popular with +53 and +49 respectively. The poll found 66% of Republican primary voters, including a majority of self-identified conservatives, want the nominee to build on President Donald Trump’s presidency, while 28%, including a majority of libertarians, want the nominee to go in a different direction. Trump has not yet endorsed a successor, though he praised both Vance and Rubio as a potential “perfect ticket” during a May 11 White House event. “I do believe that’s a dream team, but these are minor details. That does not mean you have my endorsement under any circumstances,” Trump said. “I think it sounds like presidential candidate and vice-presidential candidate.” Trump’s endorsement could have sway: 43% said that Trump’s endorsement would make them more likely to support that candidate, while 13% said it would make them less likely to support them and 43% said it would have little or no bearing on their decision. With a new coaching staff and so much roster turnover since the end of the 2025 season, it’s hard to know what to expect from the University of New Hampshire football team this year. The Wildcats were picked fourth in the CAA Preseason Coaches’ Poll, which was released Wednesday. The University of Rhode Island, Monmouth and Elon were the top three teams in the poll, and UNH will face each of those three teams at home this season. First-year head coach Sean Goldrich was a starting quarterback at UNH from 2012 to 2015. He helped the Wildcats qualify for the FCS playoffs in each of those four seasons, including two NCAA semifinal appearances. Goldrich said the expectations are the same this season as they were when he wore the UNH uniform. “The goals have not changed — (they) never have in this program,” he said. “I think that’s the most exciting thing for me is to know the standard has been set a long time ago and I’m here to just build off of that. “It’s good to know that it’s real here. It’s good to know that it’s possible. Being part of that as a player was a great experience for me and it really does motivate me, but this is a new day and age, right? New team. New expectations. A lot of things are going to factor in, but I think that the end game for us always is going to be what we want to be remembered for. What is our end game for what people are going to say about the New Hampshire Wildcats in 2026?” The Wildcats finished 8-5 (6-2 in the CAA) last season, which ended with a 41-3 loss at South Dakota State in the first round of the FCS playoffs. New Hampshire will open this season on Friday, Aug. 28, at Albany. Goldrich said fortifying the offensive and defensive lines was a priority in the offseason. “I think there are a couple key positions you know are always going to impact the game,” he said. “The things I’m most excited about are up front. The offensive line and defensive line have been an emphasis for us. I think we did a good job bringing in the right pieces to make us competitive at those positions. “God willing we stay healthy (and) we keep the culture together we’ll be able to be good in those areas. I think that’s important to being a good football team — gotta win the battle up front. Really excited about those groups.” Senior tight end Colby Ramshaw, a Londonderry High School graduate, said he’s still recovering from knee surgery. The hope is that he’ll be healthy enough to play in Week 1. “I’m progressing on the right track and I’ll be ready for the season,” said Ramshaw, one of four team captains. “Really the goals are just to be there for my teammates when they need me the most, whether it’s on the field or off the field.” Ramshaw tore his ACL while making a catch in the second quarter of UNH’s 34-29 loss at Ball State in Week 3 last season. “We expect him to play a lot of football,” Goldrich said. “He’s on track to be with us every step of the way right now. So he’s doing all the right things. We’re excited to see what he can do when he gets back out there.” Senior running back Myles Thomason was the only UNH player named to the CAA Preseason All-Conference Team. The central issue is no longer whether conditions have improved. Attention has shifted toward whether stronger margins, disciplined cost management, and steadier operating execution can continue supporting the recovery. That distinction matters because a rising share price can quickly narrow the gap between business value and market expectations. UnitedHealth must therefore demonstrate that its improving outlook reflects sustainable progress rather than a temporary rebound. Earnings remain one of the most important measures for evaluating a mature healthcare organization. UnitedHealth generates income through a broad ecosystem that connects health coverage, medical care, pharmacy services, and technology-enabled operations. This structure creates several sources of revenue while allowing the company to manage healthcare activity across a wide network. It may also support efficiency by coordinating data, care delivery, and administrative services within the same corporate platform. Current valuation signals suggest the market is recognizing UnitedHealths scale and earnings quality without fully matching the more optimistic assumptions associated with comparable healthcare businesses. The companys valuation may therefore appear supportive when viewed against its operational reach, recurring revenue base, and long-term ability to generate cash. However, that conclusion depends heavily on continued earnings resilience. Any weakening in medical cost trends, reimbursement conditions, or operating margins could quickly reshape the valuation discussion. UnitedHealth remains one of the most influential names within the American  healthcare stock landscape. Its operations extend beyond traditional insurance, giving the company exposure to physician services, pharmacy care, healthcare analytics, and technology-assisted administration. This integrated model creates a competitive advantage because the organization participates in several stages of the healthcare system. It can process claims, coordinate care, manage prescriptions, support medical providers, and analyze health data across a large customer base. Scale also gives UnitedHealth the resources to invest in technology, compliance systems, clinical networks, and service improvements. These capabilities may strengthen customer relationships and improve operating efficiency over time. Still, greater scale brings greater scrutiny. Regulators may examine whether large healthcare organizations possess too much influence across insurance, medical practices, pharmacy operations, and data services. The expanding antitrust investigation remains a major source of uncertainty. Broader regulatory attention could influence future acquisitions, business integration, reimbursement practices, or relationships between UnitedHealths operating divisions. Healthcare regulation is especially important because the company works closely with government-backed programs and operates within a highly supervised industry. Changes involving Medicare, payment models, risk adjustment, or funding policies may affect revenue quality and profit margins. Regulatory developments do not automatically undermine the companys long-term strategy. However, they may limit how much confidence the market assigns to future earnings until the scope and outcome of ongoing reviews become clearer. Legal expenses, compliance investments, and operational adjustments could also place pressure on financial performance even when underlying demand remains healthy. UnitedHealths next phase may depend on its ability to preserve margins while healthcare utilization, labor expenses, and medical costs continue evolving. Stronger forecasting suggests the organization expects improved execution across its major businesses. Continued progress could demonstrate that earlier operational challenges are becoming more manageable. However, margin stability must be supported by several factors, including accurate pricing, disciplined medical cost management, dependable government reimbursement, and effective coordination across the companys healthcare network. A strong earnings outlook may support the valuation narrative, but consistent delivery will matter more than projections alone. The market may remain sensitive to any indication that cost pressures are returning or that regulatory changes are weakening expected profitability. UnitedHealths valuation does not present a simple conclusion. Some measures suggest the shares remain reasonably positioned relative to the companys earnings profile and business strength. Other measures indicate that the recovery has already restored a meaningful degree of optimism. The difference between those views rests on future execution. A sustained improvement in margins, stable medical expenses, and dependable earnings growth could make the current valuation appear restrained. By contrast, intensifying regulatory pressure, weaker reimbursement conditions, or renewed cost inflation could make the same valuation look less comfortable. UnitedHealths scale, integrated healthcare platform, and improving forecast support a constructive long-term argument. Yet the company must continue proving that operational gains can withstand political, legal, and industry pressures. UnitedHealth Group (NYSE:UNH)  has moved beyond the weakest point of its recent market narrative, but the recovery still requires confirmation. Improving earnings expectations provide a stronger foundation, while regulatory scrutiny prevents the valuation case from becoming straightforward. The companys next updates will be closely assessed for margin direction, medical cost trends, government program performance, and progress across its care delivery operations. The core question is whether UnitedHealth can convert its scale and integrated model into dependable earnings while navigating heightened oversight. Continued execution may strengthen the case for further recovery, while fresh operational or regulatory setbacks could keep valuation expectations restrained. title: UNH Launches Statewide Initiative to Study Ticks, Diseases and the Environment - University of New Hampshire
content: As the population of ticks — and the diseases they carry — expands in New Hampshire, UNH has been tapped to lead an ambitious statewide initiative to investigate how these parasites survive, spread, and transmit disease. Funded with $8 million from the National Science Foundation, the project will bring together researchers, students, and community partners from UNH, Keene State College, Plymouth State University, state agencies, and industry collaborators to study the ecology and evolution of ticks across New Hampshire. The initiative, called EMBEDDEd-NH (Endeavor for Multi-Omics-Based Exploration, Data-Driven Modeling, and Education in New Hampshire), comes at a critical time: New Hampshire is one of the states that consistently ranks among the highest in incidence of Lyme disease in the nation — often ranking in the top ten. “Ticks are an issue that touches nearly every community in New Hampshire,” says Dr. David Needle, clinical professor of molecular, cellular and biomedical Sciences and senior veterinary pathologist of the New Hampshire Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory at UNH, who is leading the initiative. “By combining cutting-edge science with statewide collaboration and education, we have an opportunity to build knowledge that benefits both our state and the broader scientific community.” The project will focus on three important tick species found in New Hampshire: EMBEDDEd-NH could ultimately improve disease surveillance, inform public health responses, support wildlife management, and guide future environmental decision-making. Researchers plan to investigate how ticks survive, spread, and transmit disease by using advanced genomic sequencing, microbiome analysis, environmental monitoring, ecological modeling, and machine learning. They will examine how climate, habitat, wildlife hosts, and microbial communities influence tick biology and pathogen transmission across New Hampshire’s diverse ecosystems. Tick populations and tick-borne illnesses, including Lyme disease, anaplasmosis, babesiosis, Powassan virus, and other emerging infections, continue to expand across the Northeast. Warmer winters, changing land use, shifting wildlife populations, and expanding human development have all contributed to rising tick encounters and disease risk. Health officials and researchers are increasingly concerned not only about established tick-borne diseases, but also about the emergence of new pathogens and the spread of additional tick species into the region. “Ticks are more than just disease vectors,” Needle said. “They have wide roles as parasites, prey, and hosts of diverse microbes. Their varied lifecycles, wide and increasing dispersal, and status linking ecosystems and ecological scales make ticks a powerful system for studying how genomes, microbes, hosts, and environments interact in a rapidly changing world.” Research Opportunities for Students; Developing a Workforce Funded through the NSF’s EPSCoR E-RISE program, which supports statewide research infrastructure, workforce development, and collaborative scientific innovation in emerging research areas, EMBEDDEd-NH also emphasizes education and workforce development. Undergraduate students from across the state will participate directly in research, gaining hands-on experience in genomics, bioinformatics, artificial intelligence, ecology, and data science — fields that are increasingly important to the state’s scientific and technology workforce. Along with potential scientific discoveries, EMBEDDEd-NH hopes to inspire more students to pursue careers in science, technology, engineering, mathematics, and public health. In addition to Needle, the EMBEDDEd-NH leadership team includes ecological modeling expert Easton White, assistant professor of biological sciences at UNH; Melissa Aikens, UNH associate professor of biological sciences; Kelley Thomas, director of UNH’s Hubbard Center for Genome Studies and professor of molecular, cellular, and biomedical sciences; and Plymouth State University associate professor Mike Son, an expert in microbial pathogenesis. The group is rounded out by UNH associate professor of computer science Marek Petrik; Michael Palace, UNH associate professor of Earth science; and Keene State College professor of biology Loren Launen, providing further expertise in machine learning, geospatial science and remote sensing, and environmental microbiology, respectively. The Trump administration is reportedly looking to deploy a Pentagon-built artificial intelligence system to help establish benchmark prices for critical minerals. Officials will initially apply the U.S. Department of War’s Open Price Exploration for National Security (OPEN) AI pricing model to four critical minerals: germanium, gallium, antimony, and tungsten, according to a Reuters report on Tuesday. The OPEN program focuses on metals that are traded in very low volumes. Next year, it will move under the control of the non-profit Critical Minerals Forum (CMF). CMF said it works with government-funded partners to test AI pricing models and support commercially viable mining and processing projects. This comes days after a Bloomberg report stated that the U.S. was moving forward with a price-floor system for critical minerals to reinforce supply chains tied to national security. The plan, crafted by several federal agencies, is being reviewed with allies as Washington looks to shield Western companies from pricing pressure linked to Chinese supply dominance. Trump, who has been very vocal about strengthening the country’s critical minerals supply chain, recently announced that his administration plans to establish a strategic stockpile of critical minerals, supported by $10 billion in initial funding from the U.S. Export-Import Bank. Earlier this month, U.S. Vice President JD Vance introduced a proposal to form a preferred trade bloc among allied nations focused on critical minerals. The plan includes coordinated price floors to reduce China’s influence over materials essential to semiconductors, electric vehicles, and advanced defense systems. China has long dominated the processing of several key minerals and has used that position to influence global supply and pricing. U.S. officials say the new strategy is designed to stabilize markets and help allies diversify supply sources. Critical minerals companies traded higher at the time of writing, with MP Materials (MP) up 3%, Critical Metals (CRML) rising 2%, and USA Rare Earth (USAR) jumping more than 5%. title: Green Earth Charitable Organization Supports Shea Agroforestry Research and Farmer Livelihoods in Northern Ghana - University of New Hampshire
content: A $1.1 million, five-year gift to the University of New Hampshire (UNH) from the Green Earth Charitable Organization will support a comprehensive research and implementation project focused on strengthening shea-based agroforestry systems in northern Ghana. The project, Transforming shea-based agroforestry systems in Ghana for improved ecological resilience and livelihoods of rural households, will be led by Iago Hale, professor of agriculture, nutrition and food systems, in close collaboration with scientists at the Cocoa Research Institute of Ghana (CRIG). An ecologically resilient keystone agroforestry species across sub-Saharan Africa, the shea tree (Vitellaria paradoxa) is highly valued for its role in supporting rural livelihoods, especially those of women who gather its seeds for processing into shea butter for use in both food and cosmetics. However, shea populations are in sharp decline due to land-use pressure, slow regeneration, and environmental degradation. The funded work seeks to restore approximately 1,000 acres of shea-depleted farmland by integrating improved, early bearing shea trees into modern food-crop farming systems. Through participatory engagement, 400 smallholder households will be trained in tree planting and cultivation, with farms serving as demonstration sites for communities across Ghana’s shea belt. Building on prior research led by Hale that sequenced and annotated the shea genome, identified key agronomic traits, and laid the groundwork for developing early-bearing breeding lines, the project has two primary objectives. The first is to identify superior shea tree genotypes (varieties) for long-term conservation, propagation, and breeding by combining detailed field measurements with genomic analyses. The second objective focuses on improving farm productivity and resilience by establishing shea–food crop agroforestry systems on 400 participatory farms. Approximately 40,000 grafted, early bearing shea trees will be produced and planted at a target density of 40 trees per acre. The improved varieties are designed to fruit in less than five years—a significant improvement over the 25+ years it typically takes for a shea tree to enter reproductive maturity—and to integrate with mechanized food-crop production while maintaining the traditional ecological benefits of shea parklands. "In this era of increasingly short funding cycles, it's difficult to find resources to work on the genetic improvement of a slow-growing tree species like shea, despite its clear ecological and economic importance," Hale said. "We're so thankful for this opportunity to build on our decade-long work with this remarkable tree to bring practical benefit to farming families." In Ghana, project implementation will be led by Dr. Michael Barnor and a dedicated technical team based at CRIG's Bole Research Substation, while drawing on the expertise of Hale, who will serve as genomics lead, joint project coordinator, and administrative manager. The project includes long-term, multi-locational evaluation of tree performance as well as a shea conference and outreach events to share results, best practices, and improved planting materials with stakeholders across the shea value chain. “Dr. Hale recognizes that meaningful agricultural research requires local, place-based, and farmer-engaged experimentation,” said Anton Bekkerman, director of the New Hampshire Agricultural Experiment Station and associate dean of research for the UNH College of Life Sciences and Agriculture. “By pairing this with modern genetic science, he has been able to significantly reduce the time between a nascent idea and impactful innovation—an approach that enables him to deliver real benefits to Northeast producers and now promises global impacts. And, undoubtedly, the expertise gained through this project will strengthen his future work in New Hampshire.” The gift to UNH comes from the Green Earth Charitable Organization. With a focus on drought- and fire-resistant tree species, the organization aims to enhance biodiversity and resilience through science and engineering, enabling ecosystems to better adapt to future environmental changes. Medical expenses remain one of the most important performance drivers for health insurers. These costs represent the amount paid for treatments, hospital visits, prescriptions, and other healthcare services used by members. When care expenses rise more rapidly than expected, insurers can face pressure on profitability. When those expenses stabilize, companies gain greater visibility into pricing, planning, and resource allocation. UnitedHealths latest update suggested that medical cost patterns were becoming steadier. This development supported the stronger quarterly outcome and contributed to the decision to raise full-year guidance. The improvement does not remove every challenge. Healthcare utilization can change quickly, while treatment expenses, government reimbursement policies, and demographic trends continue to influence results. However, greater cost stability provides a stronger foundation for planning across the companys broad operations. UnitedHealth operates a vast insurance platform serving employers, individuals, seniors, and participants in government-supported programs. Its health benefit plans connect the company to a large and diverse membership base across the country. This scale gives UnitedHealth access to extensive healthcare data and broad insight into medical utilization trends. It also creates significant responsibility for balancing member needs, provider relationships, pricing structures, and care expenses. Commercial coverage remains an important part of the platform, particularly through employer-sponsored benefit plans. Government-supported programs also represent a major area of activity, connecting the company to long-term demographic trends such as an aging population and rising demand for healthcare services. The insurance operation remains central to UnitedHealths identity, but it represents only one part of the broader organization. UnitedHealth also operates an extensive health-services platform covering pharmacy benefit management, care delivery, analytics, and healthcare technology. This structure extends the companys reach beyond traditional insurance and into several important parts of the healthcare system. As a major healthcare stock, UnitedHealth benefits from a diversified model that combines health coverage with services supporting providers, pharmacies, employers, and patients. Its pharmacy operations help administer prescription benefits and negotiate medication access. Its care-delivery network includes clinics, physicians, and other healthcare professionals. Its data and technology services help organizations manage information, streamline administration, and understand patterns in healthcare use. This broad structure gives the company several distinct operating engines. While insurance performance is closely tied to enrollment and medical expenses, the services platform responds to pharmacy activity, care delivery, technology adoption, and demand for healthcare analytics. The combination of insurance and health services gives UnitedHealth a position across both the financing and delivery of care. title: Federal partnership helps expand innovative protected agriculture research at UNH - University of New Hampshire
content: The University of New Hampshire is launching a collaboration with the USDA Agricultural Research Service (ARS) to significantly expand a cornerstone of the New Hampshire Agricultural Experiment Station’s (NHAES) research program: protected agriculture. The new $2 million partnership formed in response to a growing need for research to support small-scale producers, whose adoption of new technologies and innovative management practices is critical to the security of local and regional food systems in the Northeast. “We see the ARS collaboration as a major step toward elevating the science that will enable Northeastern growers to make more informed on-farm decisions,” says Anton Bekkerman, director of the NHAES and associate dean of research in the College of Life Sciences and Agriculture. “The innovations and management improvements from this work will improve productivity and crop quality while minimizing risks to both farmers and food consumers.” Recent support from the New Hampshire Department of Agriculture, Markets, and Food has expanded high tunnel infrastructure at UNH, key facilities for the research partnership with ARS. Protected agriculture encompasses an array of production technologies that enable farmers to increase production, lower risks from weather, pests, and disease, and extend growing seasons. While some applications, such as high-tech greenhouses that provide complete production control, require large up-front investments, others like row covers and high tunnels are much more affordable and can be readily implemented on the small- and medium-sized farms that are prevalent in New England. Regardless of the type of protected agriculture management, it enables farmers to grow more food within smaller production footprints, diversify crops, and improve crop quality — all critical to food system resilience in states like New Hampshire, where only about 3% of the food consumed is grown locally. “Granite State farmers and growers are critical to our food supply and local economies,” says Senator Jeanne Shaheen, who supported the funding effort at the federal level. “The University of New Hampshire’s new collaboration with the Department of Agriculture is just the latest example of how UNH is driving innovation to bolster our state’s agriculture industry. I look forward to continuing to support this critical research during my final year in the Senate.” UNH will partner with the ARS station in Wooster, Ohio, which has a strong research program into protected agriculture. At UNH, the partnership will support a significant increase in the number of researchers working in plant sciences as well as providing new opportunities for current researchers. Becky Sideman, professor of horticulture and chair in the department of agriculture, nutrition, and food systems, and an expert in cold-climate horticulture and protected agriculture systems will be leading UNH’s efforts in the partnership. “It’s huge,” says Sideman of the collaboration. “This kind of support can be transformative. We’re able to hire new researchers and support postdoctoral associates and graduate students, increasing our capacity to do research. And current faculty can pursue great ideas that our existing resources previously didn’t allow.” Innovative research at UNH in the 1970s and 1980s led to the widespread adoption of high tunnels by farmers in New Hampshire and New England. Decades later, these early adopters are facing challenges with soil fertility, pest control, and other issues within the protected systems before those in other areas of the country. Ongoing research will help provide answers and solutions to these challenges while mitigating risk. The UNH–ARS collaboration will expedite knowledge and practical recommendations that farmers can add to their toolkits to be more effective users of protected agriculture technologies and management approaches. “In the Northeast there isn’t a single agricultural system applied on a vast scale—it’s not possible here,” says Sideman. “That’s what makes it both challenging and wonderful. Growers aren’t locked into any one system, so there are many opportunities to diversify and meet the demand for good local food. We’re looking to provide the insights needed for them to succeed.” Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. All rights reserved.

title: NOAA building at UNH seen as ‘transformative’ for NH - NH Business Review
content: A recent beam-signing ceremony for a new National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) research facility at the University of New Hampshire is a mile marker along a road described as “a transformative economic development opportunity.” Stakeholders in the facility — federal administrators, UNH personnel, state politicians and Durham officials — hail the new Center of Excellence for Operational Ocean and Great Lakes Mapping not only as a research mecca but also as the cornerstone of a larger development project that will drive cross-company collaboration, jobs and a broader tax base for the town of Durham. Rear Admiral Christiaan van Westendorp of NOAA’s Office of Coast Survey chats with UNH President Elizabeth Chilton, left, and U.S. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, right, during a beam signing ceremony marking a construction milestone of the agency’s new research facility on the Durham campus. (Photo courtesy of Jeremy Gasowski/UNH) The 70,500-square-foot building is being constructed to anchor an area of the Durham-based campus known as The Edge at West End, a future 60-acre, mixed-use project of academic, corporate, government, residential and entertainment uses. A traditional beam-signing ceremony July 13 gave some of the stakeholders an opportunity to describe what the facility means for the campus, the town, the region and the state. “By creating a training ground for ocean-mapping experts, the project will both contribute to scientific innovations with real applications at NOAA while also adding new jobs to our coastal economy,” said U.S. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), who worked to help fund the project that she described as being critical to safe navigation, disaster preparedness and national security. Rear Admiral Christiaan van Westendorp of NOAA’s Office of Coast Survey said the center represents “the very best of what happens when federal agencies, industry leaders and premier academic institutions unite.” “This milestone brings us one step closer to a modern hub of innovation that will transform how NOAA maps America’s waters and trains the hydrographic leaders of tomorrow,” he added. Shaheen, van Westerndorp, UNH President Elizabeth Chilton and several others affixed their signatures on the white beam before it was raised in place. Also known as a “topping out,” this traditional construction industry beam placement in an important structural area of a building is typically done to honor the workers and bring good luck to the building’s future occupants. “This building is a clear example of where UNH and the state of New Hampshire have developed sustained leadership and distinction,” said Chilton. “We are grateful to our federal and industry partners who have helped make this work possible.” The new center builds on a two decades–plus relationship between NOAA and the UNH. “Accurate and up-to-date maps of our ocean, coasts and Great Lakes are critical to maritime commerce, transportation and recreation, and directly support resilient coastal communities,” said Nicole LeBoeuf, director of NOAA’s National Ocean Service, said in an earlier statement about his group’s partnership with UNH. “This new Center of Excellence will build on existing collaboration with UNH as we implement cutting-edge mapping technology and train the next generation of ocean and coastal mapping professionals,” she added. The new facility will include office and instructional space, as well as a large-scale, high-bay area with overhead cranes for storing, outfitting and staging bulky equipment and small vessels. The center will provide a shared space for collaboration among NOAA staff, UNH faculty and students, and ocean industry partners who are expected to move to The Edge. The facility will have room to house the John Olson Advanced Manufacturing Center, currently located in the former Goss Manufacturing building in Durham on Technology Drive. “NOAA will anchor UNH’s new mixed-use complex, The Edge, which will be the core of activity for faculty, students, industry and government to come together, share ideas and execute cutting-edge concepts,” said Marian McCord, UNH senior vice provost for research, economic engagement and outreach, in a statement. “This breeding ground for innovation and invention will be a key player in providing economic growth for the town of Durham and growing the workforce in the state of New Hampshire.” Durham Town Manager Todd Selig described the event, which he was not able to attend because of a prior commitment, “a genuinely meaningful moment for UNH, Durham and for New Hampshire.” “As the first structure to be constructed from what has been largely surface parking lots and outdated single-story utility buildings, the NOAA facility signals in a meaningful way that The Edge is real, it’s happening and it’s moving forward,” said Selig. The fact that The Edge project is moving forward is important, according to Selig, not only for the research and job opportunities, but for the housing and tax base opportunities it holds. “A full buildout of The Edge is expected to accommodate around 1,000 people at any given time as residents, workers and visitors. That includes housing for young professionals employed by the companies that locate there, faculty and staff housing tied to UNH’s research mission, and potential graduate student housing, all of which addresses a genuine need in our region,” said Selig. “The Seacoast has experienced significant housing cost pressure, and a thoughtfully designed residential component within The Edge could help alleviate some of that strain for the workforce UNH and its industry partners need to attract and retain,” he added. As for the tax base, Durham has relatively few commercial/industrial taxpayers to offset what many in the town view as a heavy residential rate. “The Edge represents what I genuinely believe could be a transformative economic development opportunity. Private industry co-located at The Edge would be fully taxable property, in contrast to traditional state-owned university buildings which are generally exempt from local property taxes,” said Selig. “That distinction matters a great deal for a community like Durham. We have a relatively small tax base that carries a disproportionate burden from our public school obligations while also supporting the flagship state public university campus,” he added. “New taxable commercial and private residential development at The Edge has the potential to materially expand that base, provide meaningful tax relief for our local taxpayers, and fund the municipal services our residents and the university community both depend upon.” The economic impact of a built-out Edge could mean $1 billion poured into the state economy over a 10-year period, according to Selig. “For New Hampshire, which has long sought to keep its university graduates in-state, a vibrant innovation district with high-quality employment opportunities right at the doorstep of UNH is exactly the kind of anchor we need. Students who might otherwise depart for Boston or beyond would have strong reasons to build careers here in New Hampshire,” said Selig. Failure to restore ACA tax cuts will only make things worse, according to U.S. Sen.
